passage.title: Behind the Velvet Curtain
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
From the dark wing of the middle school stage, Nora watched the final lines of Act One. While the audience laughed at the actors in their pirate hats, Nora kept her eyes on the prompt book clipped to her board. As stage crew leader, she never bowed in the bright lights. Still, every cue depended on her timing. When the lead actor shouted his last line, Nora spoke softly into her headset. Then she reached for the thick hemp rope that closed the main velvet curtain.

She pulled down hard on the braided line, hoping the heavy red drapes would glide shut with a soft swoosh. Instead, the rope stopped dead in her palms after moving only three feet. Above the stage, the iron pulley wheel gave a sharp squeak and refused to turn. The heavy velvet curtain, snagged high near the wooden beam by a loose canvas banner, was held half-open above the startled cast by the jammed iron pulley. Down in the front row, whispers rippled through the crowd as the actors stood frozen in place.

Nora's heart hammered against her ribs like a trapped bird, but she kept her voice steady on the headset. She told the lighting boy to fade the stage lamps to dark blue so the crew could switch the cardboard ship for the island set in the shadows. Next, she clipped her flashlight to her shirt collar. She climbed the short wooden ladder bolted to the side wall.

Shining her narrow beam along the iron track, Nora spotted the culprit right away. A corner of the painted storm-cloud banner had drifted sideways in a draft from the gym doors. The cloth had wedged itself deep into the pulley groove. If she yanked the main rope from below, the canvas would tear and jam the wheel even tighter. Gripping the ladder rail with one hand, Nora turned the pulley wheel backward half an inch to slacken the pinch, then slipped the fabric free.

She climbed down, planted her boots on the floor, and gave the hemp rope a smooth, steady pull. The velvet drapes swept shut just as the hall lights blinked on for intermission. Across the dim wing, the drama teacher gave Nora a quiet smile and a thumbs-up. The calmest person in the room had just saved the school play.

tier2Words.definition: a signal in a play that tells an actor or crew member to do something at an exact moment
tier2Words.rootHint: Theater term from the letter Q (Latin quando, 'when to enter')
tier2Words.contextClue: Nora watched the prompt book and waited for the lead actor's last line before signaling the curtain.

tier2Words.definition: caught or hooked on a sharp or sticking-out object
tier2Words.rootHint: From Old Norse snagi, meaning 'a wooden peg or sharp point'
tier2Words.contextClue: A corner of the loose canvas banner had caught inside the pulley groove and stopped the rope.

tier2Words.definition: the person or thing responsible for causing a problem
tier2Words.contextClue: Shining her beam along the track, Nora spotted what was causing the jam: the corner of the painted banner.

tier2Words.definition: to loosen or reduce tightness and tension
tier2Words.rootHint: Old English slaec ('loose, not tight') + suffix -en ('to make')
tier2Words.contextClue: Nora turned the wheel backward half an inch to loosen the tight pinch so she could slip the fabric free.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"The heavy velvet curtain, snagged high near the wooden beam by a loose canvas banner, was held half-open above the startled cast by the jammed iron pulley."

Based on the sentence, what snagged the curtain near the beam, and what held it half-open?

options.text: A loose canvas banner snagged the curtain near the beam, and the jammed iron pulley held it half-open.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the phrases 'snagged... by a loose canvas banner' and 'was held half-open... by the jammed iron pulley' show that the canvas banner snagged the curtain and the jammed pulley held it half-open.

options.text: The startled cast snagged the wooden beam, and the heavy velvet curtain held the iron pulley open.
options.childFeedback: This scrambles the sentence parts! The startled cast stood frozen on the stage floor while the jammed iron pulley held the velvet curtain half-open.

options.text: The jammed iron pulley painted the canvas banner and dropped it onto the pirate actors.
options.childFeedback: An iron pulley wheel cannot paint a banner! The painted storm-cloud banner had drifted into the pulley groove and jammed the wheel.

options.text: A spectator in the front row pulled the hemp rope and tied it to a folding chair.
options.childFeedback: People in the front row only whispered when the curtain stopped; Nora is the one holding the hemp rope in the dark stage wing.

questions.provingSentenceText: The heavy velvet curtain, snagged high near the wooden beam by a loose canvas banner, was held half-open above the startled cast by the jammed iron pulley.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the phrases 'snagged... by a loose canvas banner' and 'was held half-open... by the jammed iron pulley' show that the canvas banner snagged the curtain and the jammed pulley held it half-open.
questions.parentExplanation: This passive sentence contains two 'by' phrases: 'snagged... by a loose canvas banner' and 'was held half-open... by the jammed iron pulley'. Option B accurately matches both.
questions.retryHint: Check the two 'by' phrases in Paragraph 2: 'snagged... by...' and 'was held half-open... by...'

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"Nora's heart hammered against her ribs like a trapped bird, but she kept her voice steady on the headset."

Why does the author compare Nora's heart to "a trapped bird"?

options.text: To show that a real pigeon had flown through the gym doors and landed in the rafters
options.childFeedback: There is no real bird in the gym—'like a trapped bird' is a comparison describing how fast Nora's heart was beating against her ribs.

options.text: To show that Nora felt a sudden rush of nervousness inside even though she acted calm
options.childFeedback: Comparing Nora's heart to 'a trapped bird' in Paragraph 3 shows that her heart was beating fast with sudden nervousness inside, even though she kept her voice steady on the headset.

options.text: To show that Nora had forgotten all her stage cues and wanted to run off the stage
options.childFeedback: Instead of forgetting her cues or running away, Nora immediately gives a smart lighting cue on her headset and climbs the ladder to fix the jam.

options.text: To show that the pirate actors were carrying a wooden birdcage as a stage prop
options.childFeedback: The actors wore pirate hats and stood near a cardboard ship, with no mention of a wooden birdcage prop.

questions.provingSentenceText: Nora's heart hammered against her ribs like a trapped bird, but she kept her voice steady on the headset.
questions.childTip: Comparing Nora's heart to 'a trapped bird' in Paragraph 3 shows that her heart was beating fast with sudden nervousness inside, even though she kept her voice steady on the headset.
questions.parentExplanation: The simile 'her heart hammered against her ribs like a trapped bird' (ELAGSE5RL4) conveys Nora's sudden internal alarm when the curtain jams, which contrasts with her calm, steady voice on the headset.
questions.retryHint: Notice the contrast in Paragraph 3 between how Nora's heart felt inside and how steady she kept her voice.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 3, why does Nora tell the lighting boy to fade the stage lamps to dark blue as soon as the curtain jams?

options.text: The bright spotlights were overheating and causing the hemp rope to melt near the ceiling.
options.childFeedback: The stage lamps were not melting the hemp rope; the rope stopped moving because a canvas banner got wedged in the iron pulley groove.

options.text: Dark blue light helps the audience read their printed playbills during intermission.
options.childFeedback: The hall lights for intermission do not blink on until Paragraph 5 after the curtain closes; dark blue light creates shadows on stage to hide the set change.

options.text: Dimming the stage lights lets the crew change the scenery in the shadows even without the closed curtain.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 states that Nora tells the lighting boy to fade the stage lamps to dark blue so the stage crew can switch the cardboard ship for the island set in the shadows while the curtain is stuck.

options.text: The drama teacher ordered her to cancel the second act of the play right away.
options.childFeedback: The drama teacher never cancels the second act; in Paragraph 5, the teacher gives Nora a quiet smile and a thumbs-up for saving the play.

questions.provingSentenceText: She told the lighting boy to fade the stage lamps to dark blue so the crew could switch the cardboard ship for the island set in the shadows.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 3 states that Nora tells the lighting boy to fade the stage lamps to dark blue so the stage crew can switch the cardboard ship for the island set in the shadows while the curtain is stuck.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 3 states that Nora had the lighting boy fade the lamps to dark blue 'so the crew could switch the cardboard ship for the island set in the shadows' while she fixed the curtain.
questions.retryHint: Read the second sentence of Paragraph 3 to see what the crew needed to do in the shadows.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"Gripping the ladder rail with one hand, Nora turned the pulley wheel backward half an inch to slacken the pinch, then slipped the fabric free."

What does the word slacken mean as it is used in Paragraph 4?

options.text: To shine a bright flashlight beam on
options.childFeedback: Nora already shone her flashlight beam at the start of Paragraph 4; turning the wheel backward half an inch is what loosens the tight pinch.

options.text: To tie into a double knot
options.childFeedback: Tying a double knot would trap the banner even tighter, whereas Nora is trying to slip the wedged fabric free from the groove.

options.text: To cut with sharp metal scissors
options.childFeedback: Nora never cuts the storm-cloud banner with scissors; she turns the wheel backward slightly so the cloth slips out without tearing.

options.text: To loosen or make less tight
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, 'slacken' means to loosen or make less tight, because turning the pulley wheel backward half an inch loosened the tight pinch so Nora could slip the wedged fabric free.

questions.provingSentenceText: Gripping the ladder rail with one hand, Nora turned the pulley wheel backward half an inch to slacken the pinch, then slipped the fabric free.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, 'slacken' means to loosen or make less tight, because turning the pulley wheel backward half an inch loosened the tight pinch so Nora could slip the wedged fabric free.
questions.parentExplanation: By turning the jammed pulley wheel backward slightly, Nora loosened ('slackened') the tight pinch on the banner so the fabric could slide out without tearing.
questions.retryHint: Think about what turning the jammed wheel backward half an inch does to the tight pinch on the cloth in Paragraph 4.

questions.prompt: Part A: Why does Nora climb the ladder to inspect the pulley instead of pulling harder on the rope from the floor?

options.text: She knows that yanking a jammed rope blindly will tear the banner and wedge the pulley wheel even tighter.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 explains that because a corner of the painted canvas banner was wedged deep in the pulley groove, yanking the main rope from below would tear the canvas and jam the wheel even tighter.

options.text: She wants the audience in the front row to see her climbing the wall during intermission.
options.childFeedback: As stage crew leader, Nora works in the dark wing and has the stage faded to dark blue so the audience does not watch the backstage work.

options.text: The hemp rope had snapped in half on the floor and was too short to reach from below.
options.childFeedback: The thick hemp rope did not snap in half—in Paragraph 5, Nora climbs back down and pulls that same hemp rope to close the drapes.

options.text: She needs to hang a new pirate hat from the wooden beam before Act Two begins.
options.childFeedback: Pirate hats are worn by the actors on stage in Paragraph 1, not hung from the wooden beam near the ceiling.

questions.provingSentenceText: If she yanked the main rope from below, the canvas would tear and jam the wheel even tighter.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 4 explains that because a corner of the painted canvas banner was wedged deep in the pulley groove, yanking the main rope from below would tear the canvas and jam the wheel even tighter.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 4 explains that yanking the rope from below would have torn the canvas banner and jammed the wheel even tighter, so Nora climbed up to roll the wheel backward gently.
questions.retryHint: Read the fourth sentence of Paragraph 4 ('If she yanked the main rope from below...') to see what would happen.
